hypothesis.title: postgresql query slowness and CPU saturation blocking accounting consumer
hypothesis.summary: PostgreSQL's CPU spiked to 95-100% of limit starting ~18 minutes before the alert, causing query latencies to jump from 4ms to 910ms and triggering statement timeouts. Accounting's Kafka consumer, which writes to PostgreSQL, slowed from 36ms to 968ms per message as its database calls timed out. This caused consumer lag to grow from 12 to 2,863 messages, firing the alert. The root cause is datastore degradation in postgresql, likely from lock contention or an expensive query.
hypothesis.reasoning: The alert fired on accounting consumer lag exceeding 1000 messages. Accounting's p95 latency jumped from 36ms to 968ms starting around -15m, and consumer lag grew from ~12 to 2,863 messages. Traces show accounting → postgresql calls taking 813-919ms with errors "canceling statement due to statement timeout." PostgreSQL's own metrics confirm the problem: p95 latency spiked from 4ms to 910ms at the same time, CPU utilization jumped to 95-100% of limit, and logs show 432 ERROR events and 1,296 slow query warnings (duration ~1700ms) starting -18m. The payment deployment at -35m is a red herring—payment is not on the accounting → postgresql call path, and the timing doesn't match (symptoms started -18m, well after the deploy). PostgreSQL's CPU saturation, slow queries, and statement timeouts all point to datastore degradation. This matches postmortem PM-2026-06-17 where a Postgres lock caused identical symptoms: accounting lag, slow inserts, and statement timeouts. The root cause is postgresql experiencing query slowness and CPU saturation, not accounting itself, which is merely a victim waiting on its database.

supporting_evidence.why_it_matters: PostgreSQL CPU jumped to 95-100% of limit at -15m, indicating resource saturation that would slow all queries.
PostgreSQL p95 latency spiked from 4ms to 910ms at the same time, confirming the database itself is slow, not just accounting's view of it.
432 statement timeout errors in PostgreSQL logs show queries are exceeding their timeout threshold due to slowness.
1,296 slow query warnings (1700ms duration) confirm PostgreSQL is executing queries much slower than normal.
Failing trace shows accounting spent 813ms waiting on postgresql, which returned a statement timeout error, proving the bottleneck is in the database.
Accounting consumer lag grew from 12 to 2,863 messages as a direct consequence of slow PostgreSQL writes, not an intrinsic accounting problem.

suggested_actions.title: Identify blocking queries and locks in PostgreSQL
suggested_actions.command: kubectl -n otel-demo exec deploy/postgresql -- psql -U root -d otel -c "SELECT pid, now()-query_start AS age, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state<>'idle' ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 10"
suggested_actions.rationale: Check for long-running queries or locks that might be blocking accounting's inserts. This is the safest diagnostic step from runbook RB-postgres.

suggested_actions.title: Check for blocking locks
suggested_actions.command: kubectl -n otel-demo exec deploy/postgresql -- psql -U root -d otel -c "SELECT locktype, relation::regclass, mode, granted, pid FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted"
suggested_actions.rationale: Identify any locks that are not granted, which could indicate lock contention similar to PM-2026-06-17.

suggested_actions.title: Cancel the slowest query if identified
suggested_actions.command: kubectl -n otel-demo exec deploy/postgresql -- psql -U root -d otel -c "SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<pid>)"
suggested_actions.rationale: If a single long-running query or migration is blocking others, canceling it will immediately restore throughput. Replace <pid> with the offending process ID from the first query.

alternatives.why_less_likely: While PostgreSQL CPU is at 95-100%, the mechanism is more specifically datastore degradation (slow queries, statement timeouts, likely lock contention) rather than pure CPU throttling. The pattern matches PM-2026-06-17's lock contention scenario.

Accounting's own CPU and memory are stable (~11% and 40%), and traces clearly show the time is spent waiting on postgresql (813ms of 919ms). The consumer is slow because its dependency is slow, not because of an intrinsic problem in accounting.
